newsitem.title: USA: Rains sweep into US Midwest, seen slowing harvest.
newsitem.headline: Rains sweep into US Midwest, seen slowing harvest.

text.p: Rains were sweeping into the U.S. Midwest early Monday and harvesting of corn and soybeans looks set to slow significantly over the next few days, meteorologists said.
"Harvesting of corn is going to be slowed, maybe even halted in some areas, during the next seven days," said Joel Burgio, agricultural meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.

Burgio said that during the last 12 hours there had been 0.25 to 1.00 inch of rain, locally heavier, in central Missouri and the far west of Illinois. The rain should spread to Iowa and across Illinois later Monday and into Tuesday.

Craig Solberg, of Weather Trades Inc, said central and western regions of the Corn Belt would experience a "real soaker" during the next 36 hours. He forecast 0.50 to 1.50 inches of rain with solid coverage in that area.
Solberg said amounts of rain would fall significantly as the front moves east, with Ohio and Indiana possibly having 0.25 inch of rain or less early this week.
Both Burgio and Solberg also said a second rain-bearing front would enter the U.S. Midwest later this week.
"The bottom line is that it does look like an active and wet pattern for the next week to 10 days," Solberg said.
Solberg said the next band of rain would start entering the western corn belt late Thursday and move across key corn growing areas on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.
"For the next 10 days it is going to rain a lot more days than it is going to be dry," Solberg said.
Burgio, of Weather Services Corp, said that after a couple of almost ideal weeks of harvest weather earlier this month the outlook had now turned significantly wetter.
"It looks like we are in a wet pattern. In parts of the Midwest they may not have enough time to get dried out (after the current rains) before the next rain event," he noted.
